en: The topics of debate,
the refutation of the doctrine of "universal birth" (jāti-vāda),
and [this work] composed according to my own intellect, as well as the Śruti and Smṛti, in accordance with the wishes of the Buddhas.
Setting aside modesty, some points of debate are being recorded.

Among them, first, the doctrine of "universals" (*jāti*) is refuted: here, whatever cannot be designated by way of either difference or non-difference does not exist as a real entity, just like a sky-lotus;
and since a universal cannot be designated by way of either difference or non-difference, this is a case of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
First of all, this reason is not established;
for it is impossible to designate a universal as either distinct from or non-distinct from the individuals,
because in either case there would follow the consequence that it lacks the nature of a universal.

For instance: if the universal (*sāmānya*) is intended as an entity entirely distinct from the individuals (*vyakti*), then it cannot be their "universal," because that which is distinct from something cannot be its universal—just as a horse is not the universal of a cow;
and since "cowness" (*gotva*) is indeed distinct [from the individuals], this is a case of perceiving a pervasion by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*).
Expressibility is the pervader of the reality of that which has been negated; its non-apprehension [is established].
The reason is "inexpressibility by way of either difference or non-difference.
Now, one might object: we do not perceive any contradiction in the claim that the universal is both distinct from the individuals and yet belongs to them.
Nor should it be thought that if one thing were the universal of another distinct thing, then everything would be the universal of everything due to the absence of any distinction;
for indeed, that which is a single entity inhering in many things is the universal belonging to those things.

If it is argued: "Since a horse does not inhere in cows, how can that [number] belong to the cows? How could there be a lack of distinction so that it might be a universal (sāmānya)?"—then this reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); how then could it suffice to establish the desired conclusion? This argument follows the prattle of a child. For a specific property (*viśeṣa*) must be stated by an intelligent person—one which, existing solely as a universal entity, would establish a non-confused determination. However, this "inherence in many" (*anekasamavāya*) exists even in numbers, conjunctions, and so forth, with respect to composite wholes, effects, substances, and the like; therefore, these too would be universals of those things possessing number and so on.

Now, you might think: "Even though there is a co-inherence of multiple things, that alone is the universal (*sāmānya*) which serves as the basis for the occurrence of identical cognition and designation, and nothing else.
Thus, for you, the universal is the state (*bhāva*) of those things that are similar, from which both the designation and the cognition arise.
As Akṣapāda said: "The genus (*jāti*) consists in the production of identical cognition and designation."
This too is merely an exposition of one's own internal system; for in this regard, two alternatives arise:

Are those particulars produced from their own causes as identical in their intrinsic nature, such that a universal (sāmānya) exists among them which serves as the basis for such cognition, designation, and proof? Or rather, are they indeed dissimilar? If, in the former case, they were identical by their very own nature, they would themselves give rise to the uniform cognition and designation; what then would be the use of a universal as a separate entity? And thus, it remains nothing but a non-universal.
Because, by virtue of that [distinction], knowledge and verbal designation are not applied to them in a general sense;
if, on the other hand, they are not similar, then they possess no generality,
for you have stated that "generality" (sāmānya) is the state of being similar (samānānāṃ bhāvaḥ).

How can the "Beloved of the Gods" (devānāmpriya) be considered one whose proposition is praiseworthy when he asserts that "the state of being common to things that are not common is *sāmānya*"? If it is argued that those things, though themselves of a non-common nature, become common by means of that very [universal], we say: no. For instance—what is done to them? Or rather, what is determined about them? In this regard, they are certainly not "done," because they have already been produced by their own causes, and it is impossible to produce again what has already been produced, since production is characterized by the manifestation of what was previously non-existent.

If it is argued that they are produced by means of a common nature (*samānātmanā*), then surely, how can those things which—by virtue of being already established—do not possess the status of being the object (*karman*) of the act of making (*kṛti*), be said to be "produced"? It might be replied: "They do not undergo the state of being the object of the act of making in the form of the substratum (*dharmirūpa*) in which they are already established; rather, they are produced in another, common form in which they are not yet established. In that case, nothing is untenable.
However, if this were so, it would follow that those very things are produced as a universal (*sāmānyena*) by means of that same common form.

If it is argued that even if its future production occurs from another cause after it has not yet been produced, its status as an existent essence (*bhāvasvabhāvatā*)—just like a particular (*vyakti*)—cannot be established even by Brahman, and therefore let it simply be a different entity (*arthāntara*); this would entail nothing undesirable. [We reply: In that case, you must admit that it is merely another universal (*sāmānyāntara*) produced by an eternal universal.

And likewise, for one who questions how there can be a universal (*sāmānya*) among particulars (*bheda*) that are dissimilar, if they were to admit the construction of a universal-form distinct from those [particulars], then an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) consisting of the postulation of further and further universals of effects would result, which cannot be avoided; nor would the dissimilar form of non-distinct things disappear,
nor is resorting to the second alternative preferable.
For indeed, things are not perceived as being identical by means of something else; otherwise, other things would likewise be perceived as being identical,
just like the element earth.

How so? By means of a quality (*guṇa*). For otherwise, by whatever [quality] anything might be similar to something else, they would be cognized as such due to the absence of a specific restriction. If it is argued that "others are cognized as being similar to one thing through its inherence in many [substances], and therefore there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)," this is a mere pretense. For even in the case of the number two and so forth belonging to a composite substance (*avayavidravya*), the duality does not exist as an entity inherent in one and many [simultaneously], such that the parts and so forth would not be understood in that way from those [numbers].
Now, if it is argued that there is no fault because those [particulars] lack the capacity for identical cognition and designation within their own substrates—[we reply:

But surely even the universal (*sāmānya*) is postulated as the cause of identical cognition only through its oneness and its inherence in many particulars; and since you yourself accept these two [properties] for wholes (*avayavin*) and so forth, how could their status as such be avoided? If it is argued that they are not causes of inference because they do not have the nature of a universal (*asāmānyasvabhāvatvāt*), [we reply:]...

Is it not the case that the nature of being a universal (sāmānya-svabhāvatā) consists in being the cause of a uniform cognition, and that being the cause of a uniform cognition constitutes its nature as a universal? Thus, there is clearly a circular dependency.

For instance, when you are questioned as to why things such as substances produced from [atoms]—which possess as their efficient cause a universal such as "oneness" (*ekatva*)—do not themselves have the form of a universal, you replied that it is because they produce a uniform cognition (*samānapratyayatvāt*).

Furthermore, since that state of being a cause for a uniform cognition arises from the uniformity of the cause itself, why should it not also apply to the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth? When such an objection is raised against our own position, how do you escape the fault of mutual dependence by asserting that [the whole] lacks the nature of a universal (*asāmānya-rūpatvāt*)?
Moreover, the reason [you provide], namely "having the form of an individual" (*vyakti-rūpa*), is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it exists even in the case of a universal.
It would be capable of establishing a different meaning and so forth.
This is a construction in the first person dual.

Having thoroughly examined the *Bhāṣya* of Vātsyāyana, its *Vārttika*, and its *Ṭīkā*, [the author] restates [the definition], fulfilling the intention of the Naiyāyikas: "A universal (*jāti*) consists in the production of uniform cognition and designation."
Thus; cf.
Nyāyasūtra II.2.69–70: "A genus (*jāti*) has the nature of producing a common cognition (*samānaprasava*).
It is illumination (*prakāśana*).
By its very own nature;
that is, by a common nature.
To ward off.
The phrase "they are determined" implies the adoption of a particular position; it should rather be "they are perceived.

By this, the following argument of Uddyotakara is also refuted: "Cowness does not exist in the cow such that, prior to its connection with cowness, it would already be a cow; therefore, cowness would be redundant."
Moreover, at the very moment an entity exists, it is already connected with "cowness" (gotva); the entity does not exist prior to its connection with cowness,
nor can that which is non-existent be designated as either "cow" or "non-cow."

For instance: if at the very moment an object exists it is already of the nature of a cow, having arisen from its own causes, what need is there for a separate "cowness" (*gotva*)? Or, if it is not of the nature of a cow, then it could have no connection with "cowness"—neither as "non-cow" nor as "horse" and so forth—since the state of being a non-cow is certainly not what is called "cowness. Therefore, the universal (*sāmānya*) is not a distinct entity (*arthāntara*). Since being a non-universal is pervaded by being a distinct entity, [the argument] excludes the possibility of it being the essence of a universal; how, then, can there be any inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*)? Thus, the universal must indeed be non-different [from the individual], because we have refuted a universal that is distinct from the individual (*vyakti*).
See *Nyāyavārttika* II, ii, 65.

Now, the Sāṃkhya, having found an ally in Datta, offers an objection; he should be addressed as follows: "Do you indeed desire to establish a common designation for individual manifestations? Or do you desire to demonstrate a specific excellence of the Self? In the first case, nothing is lost; we do not dispute over names.
The second position also reveals a grand kingdom of imagination;
for instance, here too two alternatives arise: is the non-difference of the universal from the individuals, or is it the non-difference of the individuals from the universal?
In the first case, the universal would possess multiplicity and unreality, just like the individuals.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which is non-different from individuals is manifold and impermanent, just like their respective individual forms (*prātisvikarūpa*).
Since the universal (*sāmānya*) is non-different from individuals, this is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason) in the form of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*).

This reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the universal’s unity and permanence are contradicted by the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*); for it is logically impossible for anything other than individuals—such as pleasure and the like—to be absolutely non-different from them while possessing such contradictory attributes.
Furthermore, in another alternative, both the individual entities and their universal would possess unity and permanence.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which is non-different from a universal is neither different nor impermanent, just like the nature of that very universal itself. And since the form of the individuals is non-different from the universal, this is a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) based on the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
Nor is this inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), for that which is non-different from a universal is indeed the universal itself.

If that [universal] were one and eternal, how could it be called both non-different and different, as well as impermanent? One who speaks thus would effectively be saying that the universal itself is manifold and impermanent;
having directly asserted its non-difference and eternity, to then claim that it appears as such only due to spatial separation—how is he not insane?
Therefore, it is established that the universal is inexpressible in terms of both difference and non-difference.
Nor is this reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

For although the universal (*sāmānya*)—which is neither different nor non-different from its manifestations (*vyakti*)—is not denotable by these two [terms] alone, nevertheless, because another mode characterized by a dual nature is possible, the Jains maintain that the universal is indeed both different and non-different.
As they say: "In the destruction, arising, and persistence of the jar, the crown, and the gold..."

People experience sorrow, joy, and indifference based on their causes; it does not arise or pass away through a universal self, for that clearly persists through continuity. Rather, arising and passing away occur specifically with respect to particularities, even when they coexist in a single locus.
Just as one may grasp whichever color one desires from a multicolored object at will,
so too, because the thing is manifold, there is the determination of both difference and non-difference when the variegated object is perceived simultaneously.
Then, through the distinction of difference and non-difference, everything is perceived;
this [world] would thus be of a single nature—this is not the teaching of the Lord.
One should accept it exactly as it is apprehended.

To this, the following response is given: Since difference and non-difference consist in the mutual negation of one another, and since the affirmation of one is inseparable from the negation of the other, how could anyone other than a drunkard or a madman maintain that these two can have a single substratum? For instance, that which is non-different from something is indeed identical to it; and that which is different from something is that which does not become it.

Therefore, one who asserts that the universal is both different and non-different from the individuals is effectively saying that the individuals are the universal and the universal is not [different] from the individuals.
How can one with a sound mind superimpose this upon that?
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is not X cannot be X, just as the nature of fire, which is hot, is not non-hot.
"The particulars themselves are the universal" is a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) based on the perception of a contradictory nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*).
If it is argued that both [the self and the aggregates] are accepted because both are perceived, we reply:
surely perception is the sublater of non-perception, but not of false perception, since even what is unreal is seen to be perceived;
otherwise, you who follow the path of perception would not have to deny even things such as a double moon.

If it is argued that they are concealed by the force of sublation (*bādhaka*), then why does the "beloved of the gods" (the fool) not see here as well this inference—which arises from a logical mark (*liṅga*) free from the three defects such as sublation—as the sublater? If it is argued that there is no sublation of consciousness (*saṃvit*) by means of logical arguments (*yukti*), is this not rather a royal edict, which must be accepted without investigation?
Consciousness is of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and since it is the eldest among the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is therefore not sublated.
If this is so, then why is inference sublated even when it possesses its defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)? If you say, "It is indeed so," [we reply: ...

In that case, this inference would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); for if sublation (*bādha*) is possible even when the definition is fulfilled, that very definition would be undermined, resulting in a lack of confidence in all inference. If you argue that it is only a fallacious inference (*anumānābhāsa*) that is sublated, then let it be so—just as a fallacious perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) is sublated by a [valid] perception. But how can this consciousness (*saṃvitti*) be sublated? If you say it is, then surely this too is merely a fallacious perception, since it is being sublated by an inference.

Now, if you maintain the insistence that perception alone establishes the fallacious nature of another perception because of its sublation, and not inference, then how could the status of recognition regarding a flame or similar objects—as being a fallacious perception—be established? For perception certainly cannot ascertain the momentariness of flames and such;
therefore, even against one's will, Kumārila must admit that it is inference alone, by establishing the momentariness of flames and so forth, that serves as the sublater of that [recognition].

Nor can it be said that only the universal (*sāmānya*) alone is thus made an object [of cognition]; for if that were so, one would say "this is that very nature of flame" (*jvālātva*), rather than "this is that very same flame. Therefore, the reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Enough of this excessive prattle;
for this [reasoning] applies to the destruction, arising, and persistence of a jar, a crown, and gold.
See Āptamīmāṃsā III.59 & 57:
"People experience sorrow, joy, and indifference based on their causes."
It does not arise nor does it perish in its universal aspect, because of its evident persistence; yet it perishes and arises through its particular aspect.
Thus, existence consists of both arising and so forth within a single entity, just as in the case of a variegated color, where one may grasp whichever color one desires.
Cf. *Tattvasaṃgraha* and *Pañjikā*, verses 1745–46; cf. *Ślokavārttika*, verses 57, 58b, 62b, and 63a, pp.
561–562, Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series.
It is variegated in color;
it is the determination of form.
Because the object itself is manifold, there is likewise the determination of both difference and non-difference.
But when a variegated object is perceived simultaneously,
then everything is apprehended through the distinction of identity and difference; thus,
it would follow that this [object] must be of a single nature, which is not the teaching of the Lord.
That which is perceived exactly as it is must be accepted as such;
thus ends the work of the Conqueror of Enemies, the *Jātinirākṛti*,
which includes the refutation of the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*).

Now the doctrine of the Arhatas is examined: here these Digambaras describe the collection of existents (*bhāvagrāma*) as consisting of arising, persistence, and dissolution in the form of substance (*dravya*) and modification (*paryāya*).

Among these, they declare that substance is the nature that persists through all states (*avasthā*); just as gold is the underlying element running through states such as a bracelet, an armlet, or an earring, so too within the reality of the substance itself, modifications possess the characteristics of arising and passing away.
Just as bracelets and other ornaments arise and perish even while the substance remains,

and just as when a jar is broken a crown is made— so that the jar perishes and the crown arises, yet the gold neither arises nor perishes— thus a thing consists of origination, destruction, and persistence, as it has been said: "This [nature] exists in the destruction, arising, and stability of the jar, the crown, and the gold."
People experience sorrow, joy, and indifference based on causes:
there is no sorrow without destruction, no happiness without arising, and no indifference without persistence; therefore, every entity consists of these three aspects.

It does not arise nor does it perish in its nature as a universal (*sāmānya*), because [the universal] is clearly perceived through continuity (*anvaya*); rather, it perishes and arises through its particularity (*viśeṣa*). Since arising and so forth occur together in one and the same locus, existence [is established];
for the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) is everywhere the defining characteristic of difference.
For it is not possible for a single entity to possess a threefold nature (trairūpya).

If, despite the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), non-difference between substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*) were admitted here, then non-difference would have to be admitted even between a jar and a cloth. Now, if you think that neither absolute difference nor absolute non-difference is admitted between substance and mode, but rather [their relation is defined by] the non-difference of place, time, and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is replied: their difference is described on the basis of the difference in number (*saṅkhyā*), designation (*saṃjñā*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and purpose (*artha*).

For indeed, there is no location for the bracelet and so forth that is distinct from that of the gold itself; nor are the bracelet and so forth at a different time from the gold; nor is there any difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the bracelet and so forth as compared to the gold. Therefore, because of the identity of place, time, and intrinsic nature, there is oneness between substance and mode (*dravya-paryāya*). The distinction lies only in number and designation—namely, "one substance" and "many modes"—whereas substance is characterized by persistence (*anuvṛtti*).
The modes (paryāyas) have the characteristic of exclusion (vyāvṛtti); thus there is a difference in their characteristics.

Furthermore, by means of a bracelet (keyūra) and a bangle (kaṭaka), the ornamentation of the elbow and the hand is performed; however, by means of gold, it is that very same [ornamentation] such as the bracelet and so forth. Thus, even the effect (kārya) differs between substance (dravya) and mode (paryāya).
Therefore, due to the difference in number, designation, characteristic, and purpose, there is a distinction between substance and mode.
In the destruction, arising, and persistence of a jar, a crown, and gold,
people experience sorrow, joy, and indifference for a reason. (Āptamīmāṃsā III, 59–60)
There is no sorrow without destruction, no happiness without arising, and no equanimity without stability; therefore, every entity consists of these three aspects.
It does not arise nor does it perish in its universal nature, because its persistence is clearly evident.

Āptamīmāṃsā III, 59–60: "It passes away and arises specifically together [with its qualities]; because it arises and so forth in one place, it is called 'one' despite its internal distinctions. This would be the case; for later, in the conclusion, it says: "Because of its oneness, there is unity."
Cf.
Āptamīmāṃsā IV.72:
"And because of the distinction in name and number, as well as the distinction in specific characteristics..."
Furthermore, the diversity of that [reality] arises from differences in purpose and so forth, and it is not [diverse] in every respect.

In this very context, the following is considered: if one asserts non-difference between substance and mode on the basis of the non-difference of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then the single form of substance and mode would alone be real. Consequently, their distinct forms based on differences in number and other attributes would be merely imagined through conceptual construction.
For it is impossible for two things whose intrinsic natures are non-different to possess an ultimate difference in any other way.

And if a difference between those two were asserted, it would follow that a difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) has been admitted; thus, their non-difference could not be established through a non-difference of intrinsic nature.

Nor is it appropriate for a discerning person to say that there is both difference and non-difference by means of the same intrinsic nature, nor that there is difference by one intrinsic nature and non-difference by another, because this would entail the consequence of admitting difference and non-difference based on a difference and non-difference of intrinsic natures.

If it is maintained that there is difference by one nature and non-difference by another nature, then a single entity consisting of substance and modes would be something else entirely, and the substances and modes themselves would be mutually distinct; thus, a single entity possessing a manifold nature would not be established in reality.
Furthermore, if there were non-difference by way of nature, there would be non-difference due to the non-difference of space and time—what is the use of this irrelevant proclamation?
For those things which are different by way of nature, there can be no non-difference even through the non-difference of space and time, just as in the case of color and taste.

Furthermore, if there were no difference between the modes (*paryāya*) and the nature of the substance (*dravya*), then, because the modes would have entered into the very essence of the substance, only the substance alone would remain. Consequently, since there would be an absence of numerable distinctions, there would be no multiplicity of numbers; thus, the plural form "modes" (*paryāyāḥ*) would not be applicable. Moreover, due to the absence of a distinction among the named entities (*saṃjñin*), there could be no distinction in their designations (*saṃjñā*) based upon them.

Now, if there were non-difference from the modifications (*paryāya*) by way of the substance's own nature (*dravyasvabhāva*), then, because the substance would have entered into the very essence of the modifications, only the modifications would remain. Consequently, since the numerical unity [of the substance] would be absent, the numerical unity [required for] the singular number "substance" (*dravyam*) would not apply.

Nor do the mere uses of singular or plural forms establish the unity or plurality of things; for we observe the use of the plural and singular—such as *ṣaṇṇagarī* (the six cities) and *dārāḥ* (wives)—even in the absence of actual difference or non-difference.

Nor does the diversity of designations follow merely from the diversity of the designated objects; for even a single horse is seen to have a multiplicity of names, such as *hari*, *haya*, *aśva*, and *sapta*.
Furthermore, when there is no difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), a difference in characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) is likewise untenable.

For it has been stated that when substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*) are one, while the substance persists, the form of the mode—which is of the same nature as that substance—cannot be excluded.
If there were non-difference between the substance and its modes, then while that [substance] persists, the modes would also persist;

otherwise, it would follow that the very same thing both persists and does not persist. Furthermore, if there were non-difference of the substance from the modes, then while those [modes] undergo change, the substance would also undergo change; otherwise, it would follow that only the modes themselves both change and do not change.
No one who is not insane would say this;

and for one who describes the non-difference of nature between substance and its modes, it is made perfectly clear that whatever is the effect of the substance is the effect of the collection of modes, and whatever is the effect of the collection of modes is the effect of the substance.
This being the case, a difference in effect between substance and mode is simply impossible, let alone a difference based upon such an effect.

Since it is observed that even a single entity performs multiple functions, difference is not established by the difference of effects; for sandalwood, the moon, and so forth, while simultaneously producing many cognitions in many people, do not experience a multiplicity of intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*). A single lamp is seen performing various functions such as scratching, cooling, and illuminating; thus, even the conventional usage of "difference" based on the difference of effects is not tenable.
By this, other [objections] are also refuted.
As Kumārila said: "For every object is distinguished from another by its form;

if indeed that which is 'object-ness' were the very same in the speech of a Vedic scholar and a Cāṇḍāla, as well as in a Brāhmaṇa and a Cāṇḍāla, then there would be identity between the speech of a Vedic scholar and a Cāṇḍāla, and likewise between a Brāhmaṇa and a Cāṇḍāla."

Now, if it is argued that although there is no difference in terms of substantiality (*vastutva*), a difference is nevertheless desired through another mode (*prakārāntara*); [we ask: would this other mode be non-different from the nature of the thing possessing it (*tadvat*), or would it be a different entity? If it were non-different, how could there be a difference residing in it?
If it were a different entity, then because there is a difference even in its own form (*svarūpa*), difference itself collapses.
Therefore, all entities (*bhāva*) have forms that are mutually excluded (*parasparavyāvṛtta-mūrti*); they do not become mixed in any respect whatsoever.
As it has been said:
"Indeed, every entity is differentiated by its form, yet they do not differ from one another;
all things, by their own nature, are established within their respective natures."

"Because [entities] partake in exclusion from both intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*)," therefore the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*) should not be maintained by the wise. The examination of the Digambara system is completed. This work is the composition of the venerable Jitāri.
Some maintain that recognition (pratyabhijñā) is a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), having as its object identity (ekatva).
